claim: The IMP2 gene is amplified and overexpressed in many human cancers, accompanied by a poorer prognosis.
source: The gene encoding the Insulin-like Growth Factor 2 mRNA binding protein 2/IMP2 is amplified and overexpressed in many human cancers, accompanied by a poorer prognosis.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by citations in the introduction and data presented in the results.

claim: Mice lacking IMP2 exhibit a longer lifespan and a reduced tumor burden at old age.
source: Mice lacking IMP2 exhibit a longer lifespan and a reduced tumor burden at old age.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work (Dai et al., 2015) and is consistent with the experimental data presented.

claim: IMP2 overexpression stimulates proliferation in human cancer cells by 50-80%.
source: Herein we show in a diverse array of human cancer cells that IMP2 overexpression stimulates and IMP2 elimination diminishes proliferation by 50–80%.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: IMP2 elimination diminishes proliferation in human cancer cells by 50-80%.
source: Herein we show in a diverse array of human cancer cells that IMP2 overexpression stimulates and IMP2 elimination diminishes proliferation by 50–80%.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: IMP2 binds and stabilizes the mRNA encoding HMGA1.
source: In addition to its known ability to promote the abundance of Insulin-like Growth Factor 2/IGF2, we find that IMP2 strongly promotes IGF action, by binding and stabilizing the mRNA encoding the DNA binding protein HMGA1, a known oncogene.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 5A-F showing IMP2 binding to HMGA1 mRNA and effects on its stability.

claim: HMGA1 is a known oncogene.
source: In addition to its known ability to promote the abundance of Insulin-like Growth Factor 2/IGF2, we find that IMP2 strongly promotes IGF action, by binding and stabilizing the mRNA encoding the DNA binding protein HMGA1, a known oncogene.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Fedele and Fusco, 2010; Ozturk et al., 2014; Sumter et al., 2016).

claim: HMGA1 suppresses the abundance of IGFBP2.
source: HMGA1 suppresses the abundance of IGF binding protein 2/IGFBP2 and Grb14, inhibitors of IGF action.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 5G-I showing HMGA1 effects on IGFBP2 levels.

claim: HMGA1 suppresses the abundance of Grb14.
source: HMGA1 suppresses the abundance of IGF binding protein 2/IGFBP2 and Grb14, inhibitors of IGF action.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 5I showing HMGA1 effects on Grb14 levels.

claim: IGFBP2 is an inhibitor of IGF action.
source: HMGA1 suppresses the abundance of IGF binding protein 2/IGFBP2 and Grb14, inhibitors of IGF action.
evidence: This is supported by citations (Diehl et al., 2009; Hoeflich et al., 1999) and established scientific knowledge.

claim: Grb14 is an inhibitor of IGF action.
source: HMGA1 suppresses the abundance of IGF binding protein 2/IGFBP2 and Grb14, inhibitors of IGF action.
evidence: This is supported by citation (Desbuquois et al., 2013) and established scientific knowledge.

claim: IMP2 stabilization of HMGA1 mRNA plus IMP2 stimulated IGF2 production synergistically drive cancer cell proliferation.
source: IMP2 stabilization of HMGA1 mRNA plus IMP2 stimulated IGF2 production synergistically drive cancer cell proliferation and account for IMP2's tumor promoting action.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figures 4D and 5J-K showing additive effects.

claim: IMP2's ability to promote proliferation requires IMP2 phosphorylation by mTOR.
source: IMP2's ability to promote proliferation and IGF action requires IMP2 phosphorylation by mTOR.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 6 showing effects of phosphorylation site mutants.

claim: IMP2's ability to promote IGF action requires IMP2 phosphorylation by mTOR.
source: IMP2's ability to promote proliferation and IGF action requires IMP2 phosphorylation by mTOR.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 6 showing effects of phosphorylation site mutants.

claim: The insulin-like growth factor 2 (IGF2) mRNA-binding proteins (IGF2BP1-3 or IMP1-3) are a family of RNA binding proteins that participate in post-transcriptional gene regulation.
source: The insulin-like growth factor 2 (IGF2) mRNA-binding proteins (IGF2BP1-3 or IMP1-3) are a family of RNA binding proteins that participate in post-transcriptional gene regulation (Nielsen et al., 1999; Yisraeli, 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SNPs in the second intron of the human IMP2 gene are associated with increased risk for Type 2 Diabetes.
source: notably, SNPs in the second intron of the human IMP2 gene are associated with increased risk for Type 2 Diabetes (Saxena et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: IMPs enable translation of RNAs containing the IGF2 leader 3 5'UTR by internal ribosomal entry.
source: IMPs enable translation of RNAs containing the IGF2 leader 3 5'UTR by internal ribosomal entry (Dai et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: IMPs bind to the IGF2 mRNA 3'UTR.
source: IMPs enable translation of RNAs containing the IGF2 leader 3 5'UTR by internal ribosomal entry (Dai et al., 2011) and also bind to the IGF2 mRNA 3'UTR
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior work.

claim: IMP1 but not IMP2 participates in IGF2 RNA splicing.
source: IMP1 but not IMP2 participates in IGF2 RNA splicing (Dai et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The IMPs contain six RNA binding motifs, two RRM domains followed by four KH domains.
source: The IMPs contain six RNA binding motifs, two RRM domains followed by four KH domains
evidence: This is stated as established structural knowledge.

claim: Each IMP is a substrate for mTOR.
source: The IMPs contain six RNA binding motifs, two RRM domains followed by four KH domains and each are substrates for mTOR
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Dai et al., 2011; Dai et al., 2013).

claim: mTOR phosphorylates one serine residue in IMP1 and IMP3.
source: each are substrates for mTOR, which phosphorylates one (IMP1/3) (Dai et al., 2013) or two (IMP2) (Dai et al., 2011) serine residues in the segment that links the second RRM domain with the first KH domain.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: mTOR phosphorylates two serine residues in IMP2.
source: each are substrates for mTOR, which phosphorylates one (IMP1/3) (Dai et al., 2013) or two (IMP2) (Dai et al., 2011) serine residues in the segment that links the second RRM domain with the first KH domain.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In RD rhabdomyosarcoma cells, the concurrent dual phosphorylation of IMP2 Ser162 and Ser164 is inhibited by rapamycin.
source: In RD rhabdomyosarcoma cells, the concurrent dual phosphorylation of IMP2 Ser162 and Ser164 is inhibited by rapamycin coincident with inhibition of IMP2 binding to the IGF2 leader 3 5'UTR (Dai et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Rapamycin inhibits IMP2 binding to the IGF2 leader 3 5'UTR in RD rhabdomyosarcoma cells.
source: In RD rhabdomyosarcoma cells, the concurrent dual phosphorylation of IMP2 Ser162 and Ser164 is inhibited by rapamycin coincident with inhibition of IMP2 binding to the IGF2 leader 3 5'UTR (Dai et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Rapamycin inhibits IGF2 leader 3 mRNA translation by internal ribosomal entry in RD rhabdomyosarcoma cells.
source: In RD rhabdomyosarcoma cells, the concurrent dual phosphorylation of IMP2 Ser162 and Ser164 is inhibited by rapamycin coincident with inhibition of IMP2 binding to the IGF2 leader 3 5'UTR (Dai et al., 2011) and IGF2 leader 3 mRNA translation by internal ribosomal entry.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior work.

claim: In the mouse embryo, all three IMPs are expressed coordinately starting ~e10.5 coincident with the onset of IGF action.
source: In the mouse embryo, all three IMPs are expressed coordinately starting ~e10.5 coincident with the onset of IGF action; the expression of Igf2, Imp1 and Imp3 is largely extinguished before birth (Nielsen et al., 1999)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The expression of Igf2, Imp1 and Imp3 is largely extinguished before birth in mice.
source: In the mouse embryo, all three IMPs are expressed coordinately starting ~e10.5 coincident with the onset of IGF action; the expression of Igf2, Imp1 and Imp3 is largely extinguished before birth (Nielsen et al., 1999)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Imp2 is widely expressed postnatally in mice.
source: whereas Imp2 is widely expressed postnatally (Dai et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Functional differences between the IMPs exist.
source: Despite their architectural and sequence similarity, functional differences between the IMPs exist, as displayed most emphatically by the phenotypes of Imp-deficient mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the different phenotypes of knockout mice described subsequently.

claim: Imp1 null mice are ~40% smaller than wildtype.
source: Imp1 null mice are ~40% smaller than wildtype with aberrant intestinal development and ~50% mortality at p3 (Hansen et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Imp1 null mice have aberrant intestinal development.
source: Imp1 null mice are ~40% smaller than wildtype with aberrant intestinal development and ~50% mortality at p3 (Hansen et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Imp1 null mice have ~50% mortality at p3.
source: Imp1 null mice are ~40% smaller than wildtype with aberrant intestinal development and ~50% mortality at p3 (Hansen et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Imp1 null mouse embryo fibroblasts (MEFs) exhibit deficient Igf2 RNA splicing and translation.
source: Imp1 null mouse embryo fibroblasts (MEFs) exhibit deficient Igf2 RNA splicing and translation and greatly slowed proliferation

claim: Imp1 null MEFs exhibit greatly slowed proliferation.
source: Imp1 null mouse embryo fibroblasts (MEFs) exhibit deficient Igf2 RNA splicing and translation and greatly slowed proliferation
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, likely from prior work.

claim: The slowed proliferation of Imp1 null MEFs is rescued entirely by exogenous IGF2.
source: Imp1 null mouse embryo fibroblasts (MEFs) exhibit deficient Igf2 RNA splicing and translation and greatly slowed proliferation; the latter is rescued entirely by exogenous IGF2.

claim: Imp2 null mice are nearly normal in size through weaning.
source: In contrast, Imp2 null mice are nearly normal in size through weaning, lean and slightly small as adults, highly resistant to diet-induced obesity and long lived (Dai et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Imp2 null mice are lean and slightly small as adults.
source: In contrast, Imp2 null mice are nearly normal in size through weaning, lean and slightly small as adults, highly resistant to diet-induced obesity and long lived (Dai et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Imp2 null mice are highly resistant to diet-induced obesity.
source: In contrast, Imp2 null mice are nearly normal in size through weaning, lean and slightly small as adults, highly resistant to diet-induced obesity and long lived (Dai et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Imp2 null mice are long lived.
source: In contrast, Imp2 null mice are nearly normal in size through weaning, lean and slightly small as adults, highly resistant to diet-induced obesity and long lived (Dai et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Necropsy of an apparently healthy cohort of mice at ~845–850 d age revealed the presence of malignant tumors in 4/6 Imp2+/+ mice but in 0/6 Imp2−/− mice.
source: Investigating the prolonged lifespan of Imp2 deficient mice, necropsy of an apparently healthy cohort at ~845–850 d age revealed the presence of malignant tumors in 4/6 Imp2+/+ mice but in 0/6 Imp2−/− mice (Dai et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: IMP2 contributes to tumorigenesis.
source: Investigating the prolonged lifespan of Imp2 deficient mice, necropsy of an apparently healthy cohort at ~845–850 d age revealed the presence of malignant tumors in 4/6 Imp2+/+ mice but in 0/6 Imp2−/− mice (Dai et al., 2015), raising the possibility that IMP2 contributes to tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the tumor data in knockout mice.

claim: IMP2 is usually much more abundant in most human cancers than its paralogs IMP1 or IMP3.
source: Herein we demonstrate that although the oncofetal IMPs are commonly reexpressed in human cancers, IMP2 is usually much more abundant in most human cancers than its paralogs IMP1or IMP3 (Bell et al., 2013, Lederer et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations and data in Figure 1B.

claim: The IMP2 gene is amplified at a high frequency in several common solid tumors.
source: moreover, the IMP2 gene is amplified at a high frequency in several common solid tumors, a phenomenon rarely seen with the IMP1 or IMP3 genes.

claim: IMP2 gene amplification is a phenomenon rarely seen with the IMP1 or IMP3 genes.
source: moreover, the IMP2 gene is amplified at a high frequency in several common solid tumors, a phenomenon rarely seen with the IMP1 or IMP3 genes.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1A.

claim: IMP2 overexpression promotes the proliferation of both MEFs and an array of human tumor-derived cell lines.
source: We show that IMP2 overexpression promotes, and IMP2 deficiency strongly inhibits the proliferation of both MEFs and an array of human tumor-derived cell lines.

claim: IMP2 deficiency strongly inhibits the proliferation of both MEFs and an array of human tumor-derived cell lines.
source: We show that IMP2 overexpression promotes, and IMP2 deficiency strongly inhibits the proliferation of both MEFs and an array of human tumor-derived cell lines.

claim: IMP2 controls the abundance of the oncogenic transcriptional regulator HMGA1 by binding and stabilizing HMGA1 mRNA.
source: Beyond its known ability to promote IGF2 translation, IMP2 controls the abundance of the oncogenic transcriptional regulator HMGA1 (Fedele and Fusco, 2010; Ozturk et al., 2014; Sumter et al., 2016) by binding and stabilizing HMGA1 mRNA.

claim: HMGA1 is an oncogenic transcriptional regulator.
source: Beyond its known ability to promote IGF2 translation, IMP2 controls the abundance of the oncogenic transcriptional regulator HMGA1 (Fedele and Fusco, 2010; Ozturk et al., 2014; Sumter et al., 2016)

claim: HMGA1 is an oncofetal protein.

evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: HMGA1 suppresses the transcription of Igfbp2.
source: In turn, HMGA1, another oncofetal protein, suppresses the transcription of Igfbp2, a high affinity extracellular IGF binding protein (Diehl et al., 2009; Hoeflich et al., 1999)
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5G-H.

claim: IGFBP2 is a high affinity extracellular IGF binding protein.
source: In turn, HMGA1, another oncofetal protein, suppresses the transcription of Igfbp2, a high affinity extracellular IGF binding protein (Diehl et al., 2009; Hoeflich et al., 1999)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: HMGA1 reduces Grb14.
source: In turn, HMGA1, another oncofetal protein, suppresses the transcription of Igfbp2, a high affinity extracellular IGF binding protein (Diehl et al., 2009; Hoeflich et al., 1999), and also reduces Grb14, an inhibitor of IGF1R and Insulin Receptor signaling (Desbuquois et al., 2013).

claim: Grb14 is an inhibitor of IGF1R and Insulin Receptor signaling.
source: In turn, HMGA1, another oncofetal protein, suppresses the transcription of Igfbp2, a high affinity extracellular IGF binding protein (Diehl et al., 2009; Hoeflich et al., 1999), and also reduces Grb14, an inhibitor of IGF1R and Insulin Receptor signaling (Desbuquois et al., 2013).

claim: IMP2's stabilization of HMGA1 mRNA together with its stimulation of IGF2 mRNA translation act synergistically to promote cell proliferation through mitogenic signaling by the IGF1R and the type A Insulin Receptor.
source: IMP2's stabilization of HMGA1 mRNA together with its stimulation of IGF2 mRNA translation act synergistically to promote cell proliferation through mitogenic signaling by the IGF1R and the type A Insulin Receptor.

claim: Amplification of the IMP2 gene occurs in ~15–27% of ovarian cancers.
source: Data generated by the TCGA research network (http://cancergenome.nih.gov/) indicates that amplification of the IMP2 gene is a relatively common event in comparison to amplification of IMP1 and IMP3 (Figure 1A), occurring in ~35–50% of squamous lung cancers, ~15–27% of ovarian cancers
evidence: This is supported by TCGA data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Amplification of the IMP2 gene occurs in 15–20% of head and neck, esophageal, cervical and uterine cancers.
source: Data generated by the TCGA research network (http://cancergenome.nih.gov/) indicates that amplification of the IMP2 gene is a relatively common event in comparison to amplification of IMP1 and IMP3 (Figure 1A), occurring in ~35–50% of squamous lung cancers, ~15–27% of ovarian cancers and in 15–20% of head and neck, esophageal, cervical and uterine cancers.
evidence: This is supported by TCGA data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The absolute abundance of IMP2 mRNA in all but a few cancers far exceeds that of the IMP1 and IMP3 paralogues.
source: Moreover, the absolute abundance of IMP2 mRNA in all but a few cancers far exceeds that of the IMP1 and IMP3 paralogues (Figure 1B)

claim: IMP2 is nearly always the most abundant IMP paralogue in human cancers.

claim: IMP2 overexpression occurs at a high frequency in human cancers.

claim: Imp2–/– MEFs proliferate at ~19–25% the rate of Imp2+/+ cells.

claim: IGF2 production by Imp2–/– MEFs is reduced by about 19% compared with Imp2 +/+ MEFs controls.
source: IGF2 production by Imp2–/– MEFs is reduced by about 19% compared with Imp2 +/+ MEFs controls (Figure 1F)

claim: The modest decrease of IGF2 production caused by Imp2 inactivation contributes minimally to the slowed proliferation of Imp2−/− MEFs.

claim: The abundance of Grb14 polypeptide is increased 8.6-fold in the Imp2−/− MEF proteome.

evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data in Supplementary file 2.

(Figure 2D, second from bottom, 2E).
